content_voiceover: This schematic zooms into the molecular mechanics of the common pathway, showing exactly how factor X becomes Xa and how Xa then generates thrombin. On the right side of the image, you see the intrinsic tenase complex assembled on the phospholipid surface, made up of the active enzyme IXa bound to its cofactor VIIIa, together with calcium, acting on the inactive substrate, factor X. This complex converts factor X into activated factor Xa, shown migrating to the left. Xa then partners with its own cofactor, Va, again on the phospholipid membrane, to form the prothrombinase complex, which acts on factor II, prothrombin, converting it into IIa, thrombin. What this image really emphasizes is the general architecture of coagulation enzyme complexes, an active enzyme plus a cofactor plus calcium plus an anionic phospholipid surface, acting together on an inactive substrate. This same assembly principle repeats throughout the cascade, and localizing these reactions to a membrane surface is what makes coagulation fast, efficient, and confined to the site of injury rather than happening throughout the entire circulation.
keypoints: Intrinsic tenase, IXa plus VIIIa plus calcium, converts factor X to Xa
Xa plus cofactor Va forms the prothrombinase complex
Prothrombinase converts prothrombin, factor II, into thrombin, IIa
All reactions require assembly on an anionic phospholipid membrane surface
keypoint_voiceover: The key pattern to memorize is enzyme plus cofactor plus calcium plus phospholipid surface acting on a substrate. This template explains both the tenase and prothrombinase complexes.
